text: First, check row counts on either side of the join. Int_orders__joined has no payments join. Fct_orders adds one. If fct_orders's count is higher, the payments join is adding rows, not just columns.

Don't just suspect the payments join — prove it. Query raw_payments directly for the specific duplicated order_ids from last lesson. Count greater than one for exactly those IDs confirms raw_payments is not one row per order.

Here's the mechanism. A real order can be paid with more than one payment method — part gift card, part credit card. Raw_payments legitimately has more than one row for the same order_id on exactly those orders.

The left join matches each order row against every payments row sharing that order_id. One order paired with two payment rows produces two output rows — a one-to-many fanout, not the one-to-one join it was written to be.
Next lesson: fixing and validating — aggregating payments to one row per order before the join, then re-running dbt build to confirm the test passes and the numbers match.
